answers.answer: At the supplied cutoff of 2025-02-24, PEP 387 is an Active Process PEP by Benjamin Peterson; all three snapshots show that status. Created on 2009-06-18, its initial accepted version was 2020-07-20, according to the latest changelog. Later revisions clarified warning duration (2021-04-16), added explicit steering-council consultation notes (2022-04-04), made smaller updates and clarifications (2023-06-26), added soft deprecation (2023-07-03), added PEP 702 @deprecated notification (2023-11-14), and introduced a five-year preference (2025-01-27). These revised an already accepted policy. The 2020 header calls Brett Cannon BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the steering council; later headers call him PEP-Delegate. The latest header adds Replaces: 291, but PEP 291 and an exact replacement date are not supplied. Post-History dates, including 2009-06-19, 2020-06-12, 2022-12-19 and 2023-06-16, are discussion history, not independent proof of effective or acceptance dates. The 2025 snapshot supersedes 2023, which supersedes 2020 within this packet. Not every intermediate revision or exact date of each smaller change is supplied.

The two-year rule was not replaced. The basic policy still requires at least two years of deprecation under annual releases, prohibits incompatible behavior changes between consecutive releases without the process, and forbids removal without notice. The 2025-01-27 update prefers five years before removal, exemplified by warning in 3.10 and removal in 3.15, matching the stated minor-release lifetime. It is neither a mandatory five-year minimum nor a removal deadline. Step 3 separately requires warning exposure in at least two minor versions of the same major version, or one minor version in an older major version; its example permits change after warning in 3.10.0 no earlier than 3.12 or 4.0. Low maintenance overhead and security risk permit indefinite retention. With a replacement, removal should generally wait until the last Python version without it reaches end of support. In 2020, step 3 said 'at least two major Python versions' and allowed longer waits, alongside the two-year basic rule. The changelog dates duration clarification to 2021-04-16; the 2023 snapshot contains the newer minor-version wording and retention/replacement guidance but no five-year preference. The old major-version wording is superseded. The elapsed-time and release-count requirements remain unreconciled, especially the older-major alternative. Authoritative clarification is needed before deriving an earliest removal date; the five-year preference does not resolve the conflict or approve a shorter interpretation.

Soft deprecation means the API should no longer be used in new code but remains safe for existing callers. It stays documented and tested, with no further enhancements. Notice appears only in documentation, which should explain why to avoid it and, if possible, suggest a replacement. There is no warning and no implied removal schedule. Subsequent hard deprecation must follow the full compatibility rules: time spent soft deprecated grants no exception or credit toward the required hard-deprecation warning period. This differs from PendingDeprecationWarning, an option within regular deprecation for extended coexistence. Soft deprecation was added on 2023-07-03 and retained at the cutoff.

All public APIs are protected, including reference-manual syntax and behavior and the C API; function, class, module, attribute and method names/types; argument and return-value positions and expected types; return values, side effects and raised exceptions for given arguments; subclass behavior, including calls to overridden methods; documented exception semantics; and exceptions commonly raised in EAFP usage. Reasonable bug fixes are not precluded. Exclusions that can change or disappear at any time include underscore-prefixed names/types, including C-API names, except special names; publicly documented private APIs; imported modules unless explicitly documented as public API; internal-class inheritance patterns; and test suites. Importing bacon inside spam alone does not make spam.bacon public. Explicitly Provisional modules/APIs under PEP 411 are outside compatibility rules. Undocumented does not automatically mean private, explicitly clarified in 2023 and retained in 2025. Public C APIs and their behavior are therefore not categorically exempt.

The steering council may grant exceptions, including shorter deprecation periods, only for extreme situations such as dangerously broken or insecure features, or features nobody could reasonably depend on, such as completely obsolete platform support. These examples do not themselves approve any change or let a maintainer self-authorize an exception. When a change cannot provide a deprecation warning, both the basic policy and procedure require consulting the steering council; inability to warn is not an automatic waiver. Council exception authority appears throughout the supplied history; the latest changelog dates explicit consultation notes to 2022-04-04. This packet supplies no feature-specific exception approval and approves no particular early removal.

Discuss the change through an appropriate tracker, mailing list or SIG, optionally a PEP or similar document, so affected users can comment. Add warnings on current main: old usage warns when behavior changes, and an API being removed warns whenever entered. Normally use DeprecationWarning; PendingDeprecationWarning may be used in special cases where old and new APIs coexist for many releases. The warning message should name the release when incompatibility is expected to become the default and link to an issue accepting user feedback. Review feedback after warning exposure, including from users absent from initial discussions, and reconsider if warranted. Complete the process and reach the declared version before making the change permanent and removing the old version and warning. For the C API, compiler warnings generated by Py_DEPRECATED are also acceptable; the 2020 wording broadly allowed compiler warnings. When feasible, additionally add @deprecated in typeshed under PEP 702, giving static type-checker users another notification channel. The changelog dates that addition to 2023-11-14; it supplements existing warnings.

The rationale is to protect the millions of applications and libraries relying on Python's core language and standard library from breakage in new releases. Backwards incompatibility means preexisting code ceases to comparatively function after a change, an acknowledged non-concrete definition; uncertain cases may seek guidance from Python developers and/or the steering council. Incompatibilities should offer a large benefit relative to breakage and be easy to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module whose name collides with a third-party package is generally unacceptable; adding a method or attribute that conflicts through inheritance is likely reasonable. Migration considerations include discussion with affected users, notice and feedback opportunities, potentially supplying a new function or method while old usage warns, and generally waiting until the last Python version lacking a replacement reaches end of support. Low maintenance overhead and security risk can justify indefinite retention. The retained timing constraints and five-year preference govern the gradual process, subject to the unresolved elapsed-time versus release-count tension.

No downstream deployment, adoption, runtime behavior, compliance, feature-specific removal schedule or exception authorization can be verified. This packet supplies upstream policy snapshots and an index of revisions and hashes, with 2025-02-24 as the latest historical cutoff. Active Process status establishes upstream policy authority, not downstream implementation or approval of a concrete change. Downstream adoption, affected feature scope, actual warning contents and exposure history, replacement availability and support dates, feedback handling, and any steering-council exception remain unestablished. Separate evidence is needed before claiming a downstream change complies. The elapsed-time versus release-count timing issue also remains unresolved, and policy after the supplied cutoff is outside the evidence.

At the supplied 2025-02-24 cutoff, PEP 387 is an Active Process PEP by Benjamin Peterson with Brett Cannon as PEP-Delegate. All three snapshots show Active status; none shows a subsequent status transition. Creation on 2009-06-18 is distinct from initial acceptance, dated 2020-07-20 in the latest changelog. Later revisions were: 2021-04-16 warning-duration clarification; 2022-04-04 explicit steering council consultation notes; 2023-06-26 smaller updates and clarifications; 2023-07-03 soft-deprecation section; 2023-11-14 PEP 702 @deprecated notice; and 2025-01-27 five-year preference before removal. These are later revisions, not initial acceptance. The 2020 header calls Cannon BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the steering council; 2023/2025 use PEP-Delegate, and 2025 adds Replaces: 291. Post-History entries (2009-06-19, 2020-06-12, with 2023 adding 2023-06-16 and 2025 also listing 2022-12-19) mark discussions, not exact adoption dates. Version and Last-Modified are unexpanded placeholders in 2020/2023 and absent in 2025. The 2025 snapshot supersedes 2023 for this packet; the indexed cutoff is not an inferred adoption date. No intervening snapshots establish dates for other individual edits beyond the explicit changelog.

The claim is incorrect: the latest snapshot retains the mandatory minimum of two years, citing yearly releases. The 2025-01-27 revision adds a preference to wait five years before removal (warn in 3.10, remove in 3.15), not a mandatory five-year rule. Incompatible behavior changes between consecutive releases require deprecation, and removal requires notice. Warning exposure remains at least two minor versions of the same major version, or one minor version in an older major version; the example allows a warning in 3.10.0 before a change no earlier than 3.12 or 4.0. The source does not explain how a shorter major-version transition would satisfy the two-year minimum. Do not infer an exception or a real removal date from version numbers alone: check both constraints and seek upstream clarification for unresolved schedules. Historically, 2020 said two major Python versions and then more than two releases, leaving units unclear. The changelog dates a warning-duration clarification to 2021-04-16; the 2023 snapshot supplies the minor-version/major-transition wording retained in 2025. Low-maintenance, low-security-risk behavior may remain indefinitely; a replaced feature should generally remain until the last Python version without its replacement reaches end of support. Five years is no automatic removal deadline. Feedback review, the declared version and completion of the process still matter, subject to council-granted exceptions.

New code should avoid a soft-deprecated API, but existing code may safely continue using it. It remains documented and tested, with no further enhancements. Soft deprecation is documentation-only, issues no warning and does not imply scheduling removal. Documentation should explain why to avoid the API and propose a replacement if possible. Later regular (hard) deprecation must follow the full compatibility rules: prior soft deprecation grants no exception and no credit toward warning exposure or the hard-deprecation removal process. It is distinct from PendingDeprecationWarning, a special case in the regular warning process. The section was added on 2023-07-03 and retained in 2025; its absence in 2020 does not limit the later supplied definition.

Coverage includes reference-manual syntax and behavior; the public C API; function, class, module, attribute and method names and types; argument and return-value positions and expected types; return values, side effects and raised exceptions for given arguments, allowing reasonable bug fixes; subclass behavior including calls to overrides; documented exceptions and their triggering semantics; and exceptions commonly raised in EAFP usage. Thus public behavior, including C behavior, is protected as well as names. Exclusions that may change or disappear at any time include underscore-prefixed names and types, including C-API names, except special names; publicly documented private items; imported modules unless explicitly documented as public API; internal-class inheritance patterns; and test suites. Explicitly documented Provisional modules/APIs under PEP 411 are also outside these rules. Importing a module alone does not make it public in the importing module. Undocumented names are not automatically private, a clarification present by 2023 and retained in 2025. The packet establishes no particular feature classification and does not supply the full text of PEP 411.

The steering council may grant exceptions, including shortening the required deprecation period, only in extreme situations such as dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could reasonably depend on, for example completely obsolete platforms. Those examples do not automatically authorize exceptions. Changes unable to raise a deprecation warning, or for which users cannot receive a warning, require consultation with the steering council; inability to warn is not a unilateral bypass. The changelog dates explicit consultation notes to 2022-04-04, and they appear in the 2023 and 2025 snapshots. Delegate metadata for Brett Cannon does not establish independent feature-specific approval. This packet supplies no approval for a particular early removal, only the upstream exception process.

First discuss the change in a suitable forum, seek affected users’ input and consider a PEP or similar document. Add a warning to current main: for behavior changes, old usage should warn and a new function or method may provide the new behavior; for removal, warn whenever the API is entered. Usually use DeprecationWarning; PendingDeprecationWarning is allowed in special cases where old and new APIs coexist for many releases. The warning should identify the expected release when the incompatibility becomes default and link to an issue for user feedback. Review feedback, including from users absent from the original discussion, and reconsider if appropriate. After completing the process and reaching the declared version, make the change permanent and remove the old version and warning. A C-API compiler warning generated by Py_DEPRECATED is acceptable; 2020 had broadly accepted compiler warnings. When feasible, also add @deprecated in typeshed per PEP 702 so static type-checker users receive another notice. This addition, dated 2023-11-14, supplements rather than replaces the warning process. If warnings cannot be provided, consult the steering council.

The core language and standard library support extensive existing third-party code, so new releases must carefully avoid breaking it. Backwards incompatibility means preexisting code ceases to comparatively function after a change; this is deliberately imprecise, with the Python development team and/or steering council available for guidance. Incompatibilities should offer a large benefit relative to breakage and be easy to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module that shadows a third-party package is generally unacceptable, while adding a method or attribute that conflicts through inheritance is likely reasonable: these are qualified judgments, not blanket permissions. Migration considerations include discussing changes with users, providing alternatives where appropriate, giving notice and sufficient warning exposure, reviewing feedback, and generally waiting until the last Python version without a replacement reaches end of support before removing the old feature. Low maintenance overhead and security risk can justify indefinite retention, alongside the five-year removal preference. The packet contains no feature-specific evidence showing these judgments or migration conditions have been satisfied.

No downstream deployment, adoption, enforcement, runtime behavior or feature-specific authorization can be verified. The packet supplies upstream policy history only, with three indexed snapshots, upstream commit references and SHA-256 values, ending at the historical cutoff 2025-02-24. It supplies no downstream runtime access or feature-specific exception approvals. Unknowns include whether any downstream system adopted or enforces the policy, a feature’s public/private/provisional classification, warning start and target releases, actual warning exposure, feedback, replacement availability and end-of-support schedules, and council approvals. Missing evidence proves neither approval nor rejection. This packet does not authorize a particular deployment or early removal, and does not establish today’s policy. Full texts of referenced PEPs 411, 602 and 702, and replaced PEP 291, are absent; only local statements about them are supported.

At the supplied cutoff, 2024-05-28, PEP 602 is Active / Process, not literally Status: Final. September 10, 2019 records Draft / Informational; November 7, 2019 records Accepted / Informational and names Brett Cannon as BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the steering council. The latest snapshot names Cannon as PEP-Delegate and supplies a Resolution link to a python-dev archive thread and a 09-Oct-2023 Post-History link. These headers establish the recorded status and authority progression; the linked correspondence itself is not supplied, so its contents and an exact acceptance date cannot independently be established here. The policy starts with Python 3.9.

The latest implementation assigns Python 3.9–3.12 eighteen months of full support plus forty-two months of security-only support; starting with 3.13, it assigns twenty-four plus thirty-six months. Both total five years after initial release, ending with a final source-only release. Full support provides bugfix updates and sources plus Windows/macOS installers approximately every other month. Security-only releases provide sources as needed, with no fixed cadence. The latest LTS section still says eighteen months of regular bug fixes, an internal inconsistency with the explicit 3.13+ implementation rule, apparently retained older wording; it should not override that version-specific rule. November consistently specified 18+42 months. September instead proposed twelve months of approximately monthly bugfix releases, a final 3.X.12 after the next feature release, and four more years of as-needed source-only security releases. That twelve-month draft is not the accepted or latest rule.

The current supplied policy has about seventeen months of development: five unversioned months overlapping the previous version’s beta/RC stages, seven months of versioned alphas accepting features and fixes, three months containing four betas with no new features, and two months containing two release candidates (or more if necessary), ending in final release. The next feature version starts development at the current version’s Beta 1, allowing overlapping seventeen-month cycles and twelve-month intervals between October releases. Late-May beta timing follows PyCon US sprints; October follows the annual core sprint. September’s heading says seventeen months but its prose says around sixteen, while its 5+7+4+1 phase durations sum to seventeen: this is a draft inconsistency. November and the latest snapshot use 5+7+3+2. They reject four months of betas plus one month for RCs because that hindered timely Fedora integration. The adjusted schedule aims to let Fedora and Python integrate while both are being developed, detecting core and third-party regressions early and helping Day 1 support; this rationale does not establish actual downstream integration.

No. Annual releases permit calendar versioning—the document illustrates calling Python 3.9 “Python 3.20”—but PEP 602 neither advocates nor rejects a numbering change. It decides the release calendar; version numbering is reserved for a separate PEP. Illustrative calendar names are not adopted version names.

The nine-month cadence attributed to PEP 596 was rejected as too irregular and too short: it would lose regular-calendar benefits while shortening development phases, especially beta and RC testing, which was considered dangerous. September left every-nth-release LTS open for debate as a possible remedy for its proposed twelve-month bugfix window. November and the latest snapshot instead say every Python release effectively has long-term support through its five-year lifetime and explicitly plan no extended support like Python 2.7. The latest LTS paragraph’s eighteen-month bugfix wording conflicts with the updated twenty-four-month rule for 3.13+, but not with the five-year total or the rejection of extra extended LTS.

No. September flagged dependent policies for updating; November and the latest snapshot explicitly retain at least two releases before removing a deprecated feature or enabling a __future__ behavior by default (referencing PEP 387), election of a new Steering Council after each feature release (referencing PEP 13), and the convention that one release manager handles two feature releases. Extending the release manager’s term to additional releases requires approval from both the Steering Council and the Cabal of Release Managers. The author’s willingness to manage a third release does not itself establish approval. Annual timing changes elapsed terms, not the existence of these rules. No feature-specific exception approval evidence is supplied.

Intended benefits include smaller releases, earlier delivery of features and fixes, more gradual upgrades with less change per release, predictable contributor scheduling, less rushing before Beta 1, synchronization with distributors such as Fedora, more useful explicit alpha snapshots, and a shorter implicit alpha-zero phase. The accepted/latest policy does not aim to decide numbering, shorten the documented support calendar, or accelerate development velocity: it does not promise faster accumulation of features or incompatibilities, only more gradual delivery. Users may upgrade faster but need not upgrade annually; upgrading every second release is described as similar to the preceding experience. Integrator changes and a testing matrix larger by one or two supported versions are acknowledged risks.

The packet establishes upstream policy history through 2024-05-28, including recorded acceptance and the latest Active / Process status, but no operational rollout status for a downstream service. The index explicitly limits scope to upstream snapshots and supplies neither downstream adoption nor feature-specific exception approval evidence. Service runtime versions, migration plans or completion, deployments, compatibility tests, readiness, service-specific support commitments and approved exceptions remain unverified. Upstream policy and illustrative schedules are not service deployment records; the absence of adoption evidence establishes neither successful rollout nor failed rollout or non-adoption.

No. The final basic policy requires at least two years of deprecation under annual releases. Five years before removal is a preference, not a universal minimum or removal deadline: the example is warning in Python 3.10 and removal in 3.15, matching the stated minor-release lifetime. Separately, procedure step 3 requires warning exposure in at least two minor versions of the same major version, or one minor version in an older major version; its example permits a warning in 3.10.0 to precede a change no earlier than 3.12 or 4.0. Release exposure, especially the major-version alternative, does not necessarily establish two elapsed years. This unresolved tension requires authoritative clarification before deriving an earliest removal date; the five-year preference does not resolve it. In 2020 the procedure said 'at least two major Python versions' and allowed waiting more than two releases, alongside the two-year basic rule. In 2023 that wording was superseded by the minor-version formulation, with generic permission for longer waits; the final snapshot makes five years explicitly preferred. Both 2023 and 2025 allow indefinite retention, or retention until circumstances change, when maintenance overhead and security risk are small, such as an old function implemented through a replacement. Where a replacement exists, removal should generally wait until the last Python version without it reaches end of support. Council exceptions can shorten the period, but none is supplied.

Soft deprecation alone cannot bypass the normal hard-deprecation process. It means an API should not be used in new code but remains safe for existing code. Later regular deprecation must follow the full compatibility rules, with no exception because the API was already soft deprecated. This differs from PendingDeprecationWarning in special long-coexistence cases within the regular process. These semantics appear in 2023 and remain in 2025; the 2020 snapshot contains no soft-deprecation category. No specific council waiver is supplied.

Annual releases aim to deliver smaller changes and features/fixes sooner, ease upgrades, make contributor scheduling predictable, reduce rushing before Beta 1, provide useful alpha snapshots and shorten the implicit alpha-0 phase. Distributor alignment, including Fedora, helps detect core and third-party regressions early and supports readiness from Day 1. The old eighteen-month cadence meant irregular dates, larger and riskier upgrades, delayed improvements and infrequent workflows left undocumented or unautomated. Users need not upgrade annually: upgrading every second release is offered as an experience similar to the preceding cadence. More frequent releases do not imply increased development resources, faster feature growth or faster incompatibility; features are released more gradually. The accepted text says documented bugfix/security support is not shortened. Integrators must adjust their practices, and supporting all active versions may add one or two versions to testing matrices. These are rationale and anticipated effects, not measured downstream outcomes.

PEP 387, Backwards Compatibility Policy, was created June 18, 2009; creation and Post-History discussion dates are not acceptance dates. The latest changelog identifies July 20, 2020 as the initial accepted version. All supplied snapshots (July 20, 2020; July 3, 2023; February 24, 2025) show Status: Active and Type: Process. Later revisions were April 16, 2021 (warning-duration clarification), April 4, 2022 (explicit Steering Council consultation notes), June 26, 2023 (smaller updates and clarifications), July 3, 2023 (soft deprecation), November 14, 2023 (PEP 702 @deprecated notification), and January 27, 2025 (preference for five years before removal). The latest header also says Replaces: 291. These are revisions of the accepted policy, not new initial acceptance or a demonstrated status transition. The supplied historical cutoff is February 24, 2025.

Five years is preferred, not mandatory; it did not replace the retained requirement that deprecation last at least two years. API behavior must not change incompatibly between consecutive releases without the deprecation process, and features cannot be removed without notice between consecutive releases. The latest procedure requires warnings in at least two minor versions of the same major version, or one minor version in an older major version: its example allows a warning starting in 3.10 to precede a change in 3.12 or 4.0. It then prefers five years before removal (3.10 to 3.15), coinciding with the stated minor-release lifetime. Low maintenance overhead and security risk can justify indefinite retention; replacement-based removal generally should wait until the last Python version without the replacement reaches end of support. The 2020 procedure instead said 'at least two major Python versions', while already retaining the two-year basic rule. The latest changelog records a 2021 clarification, and the 2023 and 2025 snapshots use minor-version wording. That historical discrepancy must not be silently rewritten. The latest calendar minimum and older-major-version alternative are both stated; the packet does not reconcile them if a major release occurs before two years. Exceptional shortening requires Steering Council authority.

Soft deprecation discourages using an API in new code while saying continued use in existing code remains safe. The API remains documented and tested but receives no enhancements. It does not imply scheduling removal and issues no warning: documentation alone announces it, explains why to avoid the API, and proposes a replacement if possible. It earns no exemption or credit toward hard-deprecation removal: any later regular deprecation must follow the normal backwards-compatibility rules, and elapsed soft-deprecation time alone does not satisfy the warning period. The section was added July 3, 2023.

All public APIs are covered, including reference-manual syntax and behavior and the C API. Coverage includes function, class, module, attribute and method names and types; argument positions and expected argument/return types; return values, side effects and raised exceptions for given arguments; subclass behavior concerning calls to overridden methods; documented exception semantics; and exceptions commonly raised in EAFP use. Reasonable bug fixes are not precluded. Protection concerns behavior as well as names, including public C APIs. Exclusions that can change or disappear at any time include underscore-prefixed names and types (including C API names), except special names; publicly documented private interfaces; imported modules unless explicitly documented as public exports; internal-class inheritance patterns; and test suites. Explicitly provisional modules/APIs under PEP 411 are exempt. The 2023 and 2025 snapshots expressly clarify that an undocumented name is not automatically private; this does not by itself classify every undocumented name as public.

The Steering Council may grant policy exceptions, particularly shortening a feature's required deprecation period. Exceptions are limited to extreme situations, such as dangerously broken or insecure features or features no one could reasonably depend on, for example support for completely obsolete platforms. These examples are not automatic maintainer authorization. If a change cannot raise a deprecation warning, or a warning cannot be provided to users, consult the Council; inability to warn is not itself a waiver. The latest changelog dates explicit consultation notes to April 4, 2022. This packet provides general exception authority, not approval of any particular early removal. Its index expressly excludes feature-specific exception-approval evidence.

Discuss the change first and seek affected users' input. Add a warning to the current main branch: old usage should warn for a behavior change, and an API being removed should warn whenever entered. DeprecationWarning is usual; PendingDeprecationWarning is available in special cases where old and new APIs coexist for many releases. The warning message should name the release when the incompatibility is expected to become default and link to an issue for user feedback. After the warning period, consider feedback, including from users absent from the original discussion, and potentially reconsider. Once the declared version and process requirements are reached, the change/removal may become permanent and the old version and warning can be removed. For C APIs, a compiler warning generated by Py_DEPRECATED is acceptable; the 2020 text accepted compiler warnings generically. When feasible, also add the PEP 702 @deprecated decorator in typeshed so static-type-checker users have another notification channel. The latest changelog dates that addition to November 14, 2023. It is additional notification, not a stated substitute for the normal warning process. If users cannot be warned, consult the Council.

Python's core language and standard library support millions of applications and libraries, so developers must take care not to break existing third-party code. Backwards incompatibility means preexisting code ceases to function comparatively after a change; the policy acknowledges this is not a precise definition and directs uncertainty to Python developers and/or the Steering Council. Incompatibilities should have a large benefit-to-breakage ratio and be easy to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module with the name of a third-party package is generally unacceptable; a method or attribute collision through inheritance may be reasonable. Migration considerations include discussing the change with affected users, providing warnings and time, responding to feedback and potentially reconsidering, and generally waiting until the last Python version lacking a replacement is out of support. Five years before removal is preferred at the cutoff; low maintenance overhead and security risk may justify retaining deprecated behavior indefinitely. These policy requirements and preferences do not demonstrate that any particular migration was assessed or completed.

By the 2023 snapshot, the policy includes clarified warning timing, explicit steering-council consultation when warnings cannot be supplied, clarification that undocumented does not automatically mean private, and soft deprecation. The final snapshot updates an already active policy: its changelog dates the typeshed @deprecated addition to 2023-11-14 and the five-year preference to 2025-01-27. It also records Replaces: 291. These are revisions, not evidence of initial or fresh approval on the final snapshot date. The latest supplied historical cutoff is 2025-02-24.

No. The final basic policy requires at least two years of deprecation under annual releases, subject to steering-council exceptions. The detailed procedure requires warnings in at least two minor versions of the same major version, or one minor version in an older major version; it gives warning in 3.10.0 followed by change in 3.12 or 4.0 as an example. That older-major-version alternative is not explicitly reconciled with the blanket two-year minimum; it should not silently be treated as a general elapsed-time waiver. Five years is expressly preferred, not mandatory for every removal: the example is warning in 3.10 and removal in 3.15, coinciding with the then-current minor-release lifetime. Deprecated behavior may stay indefinitely if maintenance overhead and security risk are small, or until circumstances change. Where a replacement exists, removal should generally wait until the last Python version without the replacement reaches end of support. In 2020 the same two-year basic minimum accompanied the literal procedural wording “at least two major Python versions,” with permission to wait more than two releases. The 2023 snapshot clarifies this to the minor-version/older-major-version formulation, says waiting more than two releases is fine, and includes both longer-retention cases. The final snapshot adds an explicit five-year preference in place of that permissive longer-wait sentence, not a universal five-year minimum.

No bypass is authorized merely because an API is soft-deprecated. The 2023 and final snapshots explicitly require the normal backwards-compatibility rules if it is later hard-deprecated. Soft deprecation discourages new use while saying existing use remains safe. It does not imply scheduling removal and issues no warning; documentation should explain why to avoid the API and, if possible, propose a replacement. The API remains documented and tested but receives no further development/enhancements. Ordinary hard deprecation usually emits a runtime DeprecationWarning. Separate steering-council exception authority still exists, but no specific exception is supplied.

No. The 2023 and final snapshots expressly say that an undocumented API is not automatically private; the 2020 snapshot lacks that explicit clarification. All public APIs are covered, including reference-manual syntax and behavior, the C API, function/class/module/attribute/method names and types, argument positions and expected types, returned values, side effects and raised exceptions for given arguments (allowing reasonable bug fixes), subclass behavior governing calls to overrides, documented exceptions and their triggering semantics, and exceptions commonly raised in EAFP scenarios. Exclusions include underscore-prefixed names/types except special names, items publicly documented as private, imported modules unless explicitly documented as public exports, internal-class inheritance patterns, and test suites. Modules or APIs explicitly documented as Provisional under PEP 411 are also outside the rules. Undocumented status alone therefore does not settle a particular API’s coverage.

The steering council may grant exceptions, including shortening the required deprecation period. All snapshots restrict these to extreme situations, such as dangerously broken or insecure features or features on which no one could reasonably depend, with completely obsolete platform support as an example. The 2023 and final snapshots explicitly require consultation with the council when a deprecation warning cannot be raised or provided to users; inability to warn is not an automatic waiver. The 2020 text has general exception authority but lacks that explicit consultation instruction. No specific waiver or feature-removal approval is supplied; the examples describe eligible circumstances, not actual grants.

At the final cutoff, add the warning to the current main branch. Warn whenever an API slated for removal is entered; for behavior changes, old usage should warn. The warning message should identify the release in which the incompatibility is expected to become default and link to an issue where users can submit feedback. DeprecationWarning is usual; PendingDeprecationWarning may be used in special cases where old and new APIs coexist for many releases. A C API compiler warning generated by Py_DEPRECATED is acceptable. When feasible, also update typeshed with the PEP 702 @deprecated decorator so static type checkers provide another notification channel; this is additional guidance, not an unconditional substitute for runtime warnings. The 2020 text generally accepts compiler warnings, the 2023 text specifies Py_DEPRECATED, and the final changelog dates the static-checker addition to 2023-11-14.

Python’s core language and standard library support millions of applications and libraries, so new releases must take care not to break existing third-party code. The policy describes backwards incompatibility as preexisting code ceasing to comparatively function after a change, acknowledges that this is not a concrete definition, and directs uncertainty to the development team or steering council. Incompatible changes should have a large benefit-to-breakage ratio and be easy to resolve in affected code. Adding a standard-library module whose name collides with a third-party package is generally unacceptable; adding a method or attribute that conflicts through inheritance is more likely reasonable. That tradeoff accompanies, rather than replaces, the notice and deprecation requirements.

No. The index explicitly limits the packet to upstream policy snapshots and states that no downstream service adoption or feature-specific exception approval evidence is supplied. These files establish historical policy text and revisions, not adoption by a production service or approval of any particular feature removal. Timing examples and descriptions of exception conditions are illustrative, not individual approvals. Adoption or approval remains unestablished by this evidence; the absence does not prove that neither occurred elsewhere.

At the supplied 2024-05-28 cutoff, PEP 602 is Active/Process. September 10, 2019 was Draft/Informational; November 7 was Accepted/Informational, naming Brett Cannon as BDFL-Delegate on behalf of the Steering Council. This establishes acceptance by November 7, not its exact date. The active header names Cannon as PEP-Delegate. Łukasz Langa authored the PEP, created June 4, 2019 and targeting Python 3.9. The evidence index supplies revision references and SHA-256 hashes. The active header includes a resolution link and October 9, 2023 Post-History entry, but their linked contents are absent: these do not establish the precise approval date or rationale for the later support change. Residual 'proposes' and 'if rejected' language does not override the recorded status.

Active Implementation specifies 18 months of full support plus 42 months of security-only support for 3.9–3.12, versus 24 plus 36 months starting with 3.13. Both total five years after 3.X.0, ending with a final source-only release. Full support provides bugfix updates and sources plus Windows/macOS installers approximately every other month. Security support provides source-only releases as needed, without installers or a fixed cadence. November's general 18/42 rule remains applicable to 3.9–3.12; 24/36 is not retroactive. However, active Rejected Ideas still says every version receives eighteen months of regular bug fixes, conflicting with Implementation for 3.13+. The explicit version boundary governs this summary, but the conflicting rationale needs authoritative clarification; the packet supplies no explanation or precise approval date for the six-month reallocation. September's superseded draft proposed twelve months of roughly monthly bugfix releases, a final 3.X.12 after the next feature final, then four years of as-needed security releases. Neither twelve months nor the 3.X.12 requirement survives acceptance. Separately, accepted/active Risks reports that PEP 101 documented only one last bugfix release after the next feature release, while several prior versions reportedly overlapped the next stable release by about six months. This reported uncodified practice is not independently verified history or authority to infer extra support.

The active nominal development cycle is about 17 months: five unversioned months overlapping the preceding release's beta/RC stages; seven months of versioned alphas accepting features and fixes; three months containing four betas accepting fixes but no new features; and two months containing two RCs, or more if necessary, ending in final. Development of 3.(X+1).0 begins at 3.X.0 Beta 1, so overlapping development cycles allow feature finals every twelve months in October, starting with 3.9. October follows the annual core sprint; the rationale places beta starts in late May after PyCon US sprints. September's heading said seventeen months, its sentence said around sixteen, and its phases totaled seventeen (5+7+4+1). Acceptance corrected the sentence and replaced four beta months plus one RC month with three plus two. The cleaner old split was rejected to let Fedora integrate the newest Python while both projects were developing, enabling early core and third-party regression discovery and prompt distribution with Day 1 community readiness. This is rationale, not evidence of actual adoption. Unresolved tensions remain: all examples run June 4, 2019 to October 5, 2020, roughly sixteen months, and their initial interval to October 14 is roughly four months rather than five. Example Beta 1 is May 18 despite the 'late May' rationale. These are illustrative schedules, not observed releases.

No. PEP 602 decides the release calendar, not version numbering. Python 3.20 for October 2020 and 3.23 for October 2023 illustrate possible calendar names; they are not selected names. The PEP advocates neither for nor against renumbering and leaves that decision to a separate PEP. Acceptance of annual releases does not authorize calendar versioning. The later terminology change from 'major' to 'feature' versions is not a numbering decision.

The nine-month cadence attributed to PEP 596 was rejected as too irregular and too short: it would lose the benefits of a regular annual calendar while shortening development phases, especially beta and RC testing, which was considered dangerous. September particularly highlighted beta shortening. September also left Python-2.7-style LTS for every n-th release open for debate to mitigate the inconvenience of twelve-month bugfix support while limiting core maintenance cost. Acceptance superseded that open option: each release already has five years of support, and no extended support in the vein of Python 2.7 is planned. No n or special LTS terms was approved. The active text retains this decision, but its eighteen-month regular-bugfix rationale conflicts with Implementation's 24 months from 3.13. The no-extended-LTS position is clear; that duration explanation remains unreconciled.

No. The draft's unspecified update list was replaced by explicit retained rules. As PEP 602 describes PEP 387, at least two releases must precede removal of a deprecated feature or enabling a __future__ behavior by default. This is a minimum release count, not automatic removal at release two or a newly inferred elapsed-time rule. PEP 13's election of a new Steering Council after each feature release remains. A Release Manager retains the convention of handling two feature releases; extension to more requires approval from both the Steering Council and the Cabal of Release Managers. The author's willingness to manage a third release is not evidence of approval. Additional RCs are permitted if necessary, but do not waive Beta 1's feature freeze. Other implicit timing dependencies remain possible. Referenced PEP texts, actual governance practice and feature-specific exception approvals are absent.

Intended benefits are smaller releases, earlier delivery of features and fixes, a more gradual upgrade path, predictable contributor scheduling, less pressure to rush before Beta 1, more meaningful explicit alpha snapshots, less implicit 'alpha 0' overlap, and distributor alignment that finds regressions early. The policy does not assume more development resources or accelerate development velocity: Python is not intended to gain features or incompatibilities faster; changes reach users more gradually. Users may upgrade faster but need not upgrade every release; upgrading every second release is offered as an experience similar to the preceding cadence. Version renumbering is a separate non-goal. The accepted text says documented bugfix and security support are not shortened; the active support split must nevertheless be read by version. These are stated intentions, not measured outcomes. Integrators must adjust their practices, and maintainers supporting all active versions eventually face one or two additional versions in their testing matrices.

The packet establishes upstream policy history only: acceptance by November 7, 2019 and Active/Process status at May 28, 2024, with version-specific support rules. It establishes no downstream service rollout status: adoption could be planned, underway, complete or absent, and this evidence cannot distinguish them. No service deployment records, runtime behavior or versions, migration results, compatibility validation, actual release observations, or feature-specific exception approvals are supplied. Acceptance and illustrative schedules are not operational evidence. Linked discussions/resolution, referenced figures and other PEP texts are also absent. Service-specific evidence is required to verify rollout; policy and practice after this cutoff are unverified.
